patient.chief_complaint: Three months of rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness, foot drop, and difficulty with arm elevation
patient.history_present_illness: Angela Rosario is a 42-year-old nurse who presents to urgent neurology clinic with a 3-month history of rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness. The symptoms began with right foot drop that developed over 1 week, followed by left foot weakness 3 weeks later. She now has difficulty raising her arms above shoulder height and reports bilateral grip weakness. She is considering stopping work as an ICU nurse due to difficulty carrying equipment. She reports associated diffuse myalgia, fatigue, and proximal arm aching. She was evaluated in her own ED 6 weeks ago with labs showing markedly elevated CK (4,800 U/L), and was told she may have 'some kind of muscle problem' and to follow up with neurology. She was empirically started on a 5-day prednisone taper by her primary care physician, which gave modest temporary improvement but symptoms recurred within 2 weeks. She notes her eyelids are slightly heavy, particularly at the end of long shifts, though no diplopia. She has had some difficulty swallowing solids over the past 4 weeks. She recently completed a 6-week course of atorvastatin 40 mg (started 4 months ago) before suspending it herself after reading about statin myopathy. A prior EMG ordered by her primary care was interpreted as 'neuropathic' by the technician (not a physician) and she was told to see neurology for neuropathy — but she suspects this is wrong given her muscle symptoms.

specialized_test.impression: NORMAL NCS. Motor and sensory nerve conduction velocities, amplitudes, and distal latencies within normal limits bilaterally. No evidence of demyelination or axonal loss on nerve conduction studies. EMG: short-duration, low-amplitude, polyphasic motor unit potentials with early recruitment — myopathic pattern. Fibrillation potentials present in proximal muscles bilaterally. Findings indicate a myopathic process; no electrophysiological evidence of peripheral neuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Muscle biopsy left deltoid: POLYMYOSITIS PATTERN. Endomysial CD8+ T lymphocyte infiltration invading non-necrotic muscle fibers. MHC class I upregulation on all fibers. Multifocal myofiber necrosis and regeneration (perifascicular pattern absent — not dermatomyositis). No perifascicular atrophy.

report.summary: HRCT CHEST: Bilateral lower lobe predominant reticulation with ground glass opacities (GGO). Traction bronchiectasis bilateral lower lobes. Subpleural sparing partially present. Pattern: NONSPECIFIC INTERSTITIAL PNEUMONIA (NSIP) — the most common ILD pattern in anti-synthetase syndrome. No honeycombing (not UIP pattern). No consolidation.
report.interpretation: Bilateral lower lobe predominant reticulation and ground glass opacities with traction bronchiectasis, predominantly subpleural distribution. Pattern consistent with nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP). No honeycombing. No consolidation. Clinical correlation recommended.

report.summary: CT CHEST/ABDOMEN/PELVIS: HRCT chest — NSIP pattern ILD (as above), no malignancy. Abdomen/pelvis: No mass, no lymphadenopathy, no organ abnormality. IMPRESSION: No occult malignancy identified. Anti-Jo-1 anti-synthetase syndrome has lower cancer association than anti-TIF1-gamma dermatomyositis (which has >50% cancer risk). Standard cancer screening (mammogram, Pap, colonoscopy) should be current. No specific malignancy workup beyond age-appropriate screening required for anti-Jo-1.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Anti-synthetase syndrome (anti-Jo-1 polymyositis with ILD) — misattributed to peripheral neuropathy
critical_actions: Do NOT accept 'neuropathy' diagnosis when CK is 4800 U/L and weakness is proximal predominant — this is myopathy
Repeat NCS/EMG with physician interpretation — myopathic MUPs were misread as neuropathic by non-physician technician
Order anti-Jo-1 and full myositis antibody panel — this is the primary diagnostic test
Order HRCT chest urgently — ILD can be rapidly progressive in anti-synthetase syndrome and causes significant morbidity/mortality
Evaluate for MG overlap (ptosis, dysphagia) — AChR antibody and RNS
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose as peripheral neuropathy based on misread EMG — normal NCS excludes significant neuropathy
Do not attribute to statin myopathy without checking anti-HMGCR — statin was 4 months only; primary diagnosis is anti-synthetase syndrome
Do not miss ILD evaluation — 80-90% of anti-synthetase syndrome patients have ILD which is the leading cause of death
Do not use ice pack test result to diagnose MG without AChR/MuSK antibodies — ice pack test is non-specific and can be positive in any cause of ptosis

differential.key_features: Normal NCS; myopathic not neuropathic EMG; weakness is proximal predominant (deltoids, hip flexors) not distal; no sensory loss; CK markedly elevated (neuropathy does not elevate CK significantly)
Anti-HMGCR negative; anti-SRP negative; statin was only 4 months (short duration); biopsy shows inflammatory cells invading fibers (PM pattern) not pure necrosis (IMNM pattern)
Ptosis from levator myositis not NMJ dysfunction; AChR/MuSK antibodies negative; no decremental response on RNS; ice pack test can be false positive in non-MG ptosis

No classic skin rash (Gottron's papules, heliotrope, V-sign, shawl sign — all absent); no perifascicular atrophy on biopsy; anti-Mi-2 and anti-TIF1-gamma negative; anti-Jo-1 positive (more typical of PM/antisynthetase)

key_reasoning_points: DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE: Three compounding misdirections — (1) non-physician EMG misread myopathic MUPs as neuropathic, (2) atorvastatin history led to statin myopathy attribution, (3) ptosis/dysphagia raised false MG concern
CRITICAL CLUE IGNORED: CK 4,800 U/L (18x ULN) — peripheral neuropathy does NOT elevate CK; only myopathy or motor neuron disease elevates CK significantly
PROXIMAL WEAKNESS DISTRIBUTION: Deltoids 3+/5, hip flexors 3+/5 with intact sensation = myopathy; typical neuropathy has distal > proximal and sensory + motor
EMG PITFALL: Myopathic MUPs (small, short, polyphasic) can be mistaken for neuropathic by inexperienced readers; expert physician interpretation is essential
ANTI-JO-1 CLINICAL SYNDROME: Not just myositis — includes ILD (90%), Raynaud's, inflammatory arthritis, mechanic's hands; must evaluate all components
ICE PACK TEST: Positive in any ptosis (cold improves acetylcholinesterase activity) — non-specific for MG; AChR antibody and RNS are the definitive tests
STATIN TRAP: 4 months of atorvastatin + elevated CK = statin myopathy assumption; anti-HMGCR must be checked; in this case, statin was coincidental (pre-existing anti-Jo-1 syndrome)
